title: Physics: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank

toc.title: 2.21 Potential, potential difference and potential energy

html:
Group A of the NEB Grade 11 Physics paper is eleven one-mark multiple-choice questions — eleven marks, and the only eleven marks in the paper you can secure in under fifteen minutes. This chapter drills all twenty-six syllabus units in order. Each section opens with a high-yield facts table (the constants and formulae the objective questions keep returning to), then gives eight MCQs, then an answer key in which every answer carries a one-line reason and, where a wrong option encodes a real misconception, names it.

What Group A actually tests

Almost nothing in Group A is a long calculation. It tests four things: a definition, a unit or dimension, a direct substitution into one formula, or a misconception deliberately offered as a distractor. If an MCQ is taking you more than ninety seconds, you have misread it.

No question here carries a year tag — and that is deliberate

Coaching sites circulate lists labelled "NEB 2078", "NEB 2081" and so on, but NEB does not publish its Grade 11 question papers, and we could not verify a single item against an official released paper. Rather than print a year we cannot stand behind, we print none. What we can stand behind is the syllabus weighting, which is public, and every question below is built from it. Treat this as a bank of exam-shaped questions, not a leaked paper.

2.1 Physical Quantities

High-yield fact Value / form
Force [MLT^{-2}], newton
Work, energy, torque [ML^{2}T^{-2}]
Power [ML^{2}T^{-3}], watt
Pressure, stress, all elastic moduli, energy density [ML^{-1}T^{-2}], pascal
Planck constant, angular momentum [ML^{2}T^{-1}]
Gravitational constant G [M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}]
Dimensionless quantities strain, refractive index, relative density, angle, \mu, Poisson's ratio, dielectric constant
Vernier least count \text{L.C.} = 1\ \text{MSD} - 1\ \text{VSD}
Screw gauge least count pitch \div number of circular-scale divisions
Error in Z = A^{p}B^{q}/C^{r} \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = p\frac{\Delta A}{A} + q\frac{\Delta B}{B} + r\frac{\Delta C}{C}
  1. The dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant G is [1]a[M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}]b[ML^{3}T^{-2}]c[M^{-1}L^{2}T^{-2}]d[ML^{2}T^{-2}]
  2. Which pair does not have the same dimensions? [1]awork and torquebimpulse and momentumcstress and pressuredforce and power
  3. The number of significant figures in 0.002340 is [1]a7b6c4d3
  4. Ten divisions of a vernier scale coincide with nine divisions of the main scale, and 1\ \text{MSD} = 1\ \text{mm}. The least count is [1]a0.1\ \text{mm}b0.01\ \text{mm}c1\ \text{mm}d0.05\ \text{mm}
  5. Which quantity is dimensionless yet is given a unit? [1]aplane anglebstraincrefractive indexdrelative density
  6. Dimensional analysis cannot be used to find [1]awhether an equation is dimensionally correctbthe value of a dimensionless constantcthe conversion factor between two systems of unitsdthe dimensions of a derived quantity
  7. If Z = A^{2}B^{3}/C and the percentage errors in A, B and C are 1\%, 2\% and 3\%, the percentage error in Z is [1]a6\%b8\%c10\%d11\%
  8. The dimensional formula [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] belongs to [1]asurface tensionbpressurecforce constantdlinear momentum
Answers — 2.1

1. (a) — from F = Gm_1m_2/r^2, G = Fr^2/m^2 gives [MLT^{-2}][L^2][M^{-2}] = [M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}].

2. (d) — force is [MLT^{-2}], power is [ML^{2}T^{-3}]. Distractor (a) tempts students who think "torque is not energy so its dimensions must differ"; they are identical, only the physical meaning differs.

3. (c) — leading zeros are never significant, the trailing zero after the decimal point is; so 2, 3, 4, 0 = four.

4. (a) — 10\ \text{VSD} = 9\ \text{MSD}, so 1\ \text{VSD} = 0.9\ \text{mm} and \text{L.C.} = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1\ \text{mm}. Option (b) is the screw-gauge least count, quoted from memory.

5. (a) — angle is length/length, so dimensionless, but SI still names the radian for it.

6. (b) — the method matches powers of M, L, T; a pure number carries none, so it survives undetermined.

7. (d) — 2(1) + 3(2) + 1(3) = 11\%. Option (a) comes from adding the errors without their powers; (c) from forgetting the C term.

8. (b) — pressure is force per area. Surface tension and force constant are both [MT^{-2}], momentum is [MLT^{-1}].

2.2 Vectors

High-yield fact Value / form
Resultant (parallelogram law) R = \sqrt{P^{2}+Q^{2}+2PQ\cos\theta}
Direction of resultant \tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}
Maximum, minimum resultant P+Q at \theta = 0^{\circ}; |P-Q| at \theta = 180^{\circ}
Scalar product \vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta — a scalar
Vector product |\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta — a vector, \perp to both
Unit-vector rules \hat i\cdot\hat i = 1, \hat i\times\hat i = 0, \hat i\times\hat j = \hat k
Resolution A_x = A\cos\theta, A_y = A\sin\theta
  1. Two equal vectors of magnitude P act at 120^{\circ} to each other. Their resultant has magnitude [1]a2PbP\sqrt{3}cPdzero
  2. Forces of 3\ \text{N} and 4\ \text{N} act at right angles. The resultant is [1]a1\ \text{N}b5\ \text{N}c7\ \text{N}d12\ \text{N}
  3. The minimum number of coplanar vectors of unequal magnitude whose resultant can be zero is [1]a2b3c4d5
  4. If \vec A\cdot\vec B = 0 and neither vector is zero, the angle between them is [1]a0^{\circ}b45^{\circ}c90^{\circ}d180^{\circ}
  5. \hat i\times\hat j is equal to [1]a0b1c\hat kd-\hat k
  6. The vector product of two parallel vectors is [1]amaximumbzerocunitydinfinite
  7. A vector of magnitude 10 units makes 60^{\circ} with the x-axis. Its x-component is [1]a5 unitsb5\sqrt{3} unitsc10 unitsd8.66 units
  8. Which of the following is a scalar quantity? [1]atorquebimpulsecworkdangular velocity
Answers — 2.2

1. (c) — R = \sqrt{P^2+P^2+2P^2\cos120^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2P^2-P^2} = P. Option (a) is the answer for 0^{\circ}; students who forget that \cos120^{\circ} is negative pick it.

2. (b) — \sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5. Option (c) adds the magnitudes, the commonest vector error of all.

3. (b) — two unequal vectors can never cancel; three can, if they close a triangle.

4. (c) — AB\cos\theta = 0 with A,B \ne 0 forces \cos\theta = 0.

5. (c) — right-hand rule, in cyclic order \hat i\to\hat j\to\hat k. Option (d) is \hat j\times\hat i, the order reversed.

6. (b) — \sin 0^{\circ} = 0. Option (a) is true of the scalar product; that swap is the classic confusion.

7. (a) — A_x = 10\cos60^{\circ} = 5. Option (d) is 10\sin60^{\circ}, sine and cosine swapped.

8. (c) — work is \vec F\cdot\vec s, a scalar product. The other three are vectors.

2.3 Kinematics

High-yield fact Value / form
Equations of motion v = u+at, s = ut+\tfrac12at^{2}, v^{2} = u^{2}+2as
Distance in the n^{\text{th}} second s_n = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n-1) — a distance, unit metre
Slope and area x–t slope = v; v–t slope = a, v–t area = s
Projectile T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}, H = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g}, R = \dfrac{u^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}
Maximum range R_{\max} = u^{2}/g at \theta = 45^{\circ}; \theta and 90^{\circ}-\theta give equal range
Speed at the top u\cos\theta, not zero
Horizontal projection t = \sqrt{2h/g}, independent of u
Relative velocity \vec v_{AB} = \vec v_A - \vec v_B

  1. From the velocity–time graph above, the total displacement of the body in 10\ \text{s} is [1]a100\ \text{m}b120\ \text{m}c140\ \text{m}d200\ \text{m}
  2. The area under an acceleration–time graph gives [1]adisplacementbchange in velocitycaverage velocitydjerk
  3. At the highest point of its trajectory, the velocity of a projectile is [1]azerobvertical and equal to u\sin\thetachorizontal and equal to u\cos\thetadequal to u
  4. A stone is dropped from a height and another is thrown horizontally from the same height at the same instant. They [1]areach the ground togetherbthe dropped one lands firstcthe thrown one lands firstdit depends on the mass
  5. For a freely falling body starting from rest, the distances covered in the first, second and third seconds are in the ratio [1]a1:2:3b1:3:5c1:4:9d1:1:1
  6. Two cars move towards each other at 10\ \text{m s}^{-1} and 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}. The speed of one relative to the other is [1]a10\ \text{m s}^{-1}b15\ \text{m s}^{-1}c30\ \text{m s}^{-1}d200\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  7. A body is projected with speed u at 30^{\circ}. Another has the same range with the same speed at [1]a45^{\circ}b60^{\circ}c75^{\circ}d120^{\circ}
  8. The quantity s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1) has the SI unit [1]a\text{m s}^{-1}b\text{m s}^{-2}c\text{m}d\text{m s}
Answers — 2.3

1. (c) — triangle A = \tfrac12(4)(20) = 40, rectangle B = 4\times20 = 80, triangle C = \tfrac12(2)(20) = 20; total 140\ \text{m}. Option (d) is 20\times10, the area of the whole rectangle — the error of treating a varying velocity as constant.

2. (b) — area = \int a\,dt = \Delta v. Option (a) is the area under a velocity–time graph; mixing the two graphs up is the standard slip.

3. (c) — only the vertical component vanishes.

4. (a) — vertical motion is identical and independent of the horizontal motion; t = \sqrt{2h/g} contains no u.

5. (b) — s_n \propto (2n-1), giving 1:3:5. Option (c) is the ratio of total distances after 1, 2, 3 s.

6. (c) — opposite directions, so v_{AB} = 10-(-20) = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}. Option (a) subtracts the speeds, which is right only for the same direction.

7. (b) — complementary angles give equal range, and 90^{\circ}-30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}.

8. (c) — it is the distance travelled during one particular second, so a metre. The "per second" in the wording tempts (a).

How to kill a projectile MCQ in twenty seconds

Problem. A ball thrown at 20\ \text{m s}^{-1} at 30^{\circ} (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}) has range (a) 20\ \text{m} (b) 34.6\ \text{m} (c) 40\ \text{m} (d) 10\ \text{m}.

Solution. Do not compute components. Go straight to R = u^{2}\sin2\theta/g with 2\theta = 60^{\circ}:

R = \frac{(20)^{2}\sin60^{\circ}}{10} = \frac{400 \times 0.866}{10} = 34.6\ \text{m}

Answer (b). Option (c) is u^{2}/g, the maximum range — offered to anyone who reaches for 45^{\circ} out of habit.

2.4 Dynamics

High-yield fact Value / form
Newton's second law \vec F = \dfrac{d\vec p}{dt} = m\vec a
Impulse \vec J = \vec F_{av}\Delta t = m\vec v - m\vec u, unit N s = kg m s⁻¹
Conservation of momentum m_1u_1+m_2u_2 = m_1v_1+m_2v_2 (no external force)
Torque \tau = F\,d_\perp = rF\sin\theta, unit N m
Friction \mu_s = f_{lim}/N, \mu_k = f_k/N, and \mu_k < \mu_s
Angle of repose \mu_s = \tan\theta — equals the angle of friction \lambda
Body on a smooth incline a = g\sin\theta, N = mg\cos\theta
Lift apparent weight = m(g+a) going up, m(g-a) going down

  1. Newton's second law of motion in its most general form is [1]aF = mvbF = dp/dtcF = ma onlydF = mg
  2. The SI unit of impulse is the same as that of [1]aforcebenergyclinear momentumdpower
  3. A rocket moves forward because [1]athe exhaust gases push against the airbof conservation of linear momentumcof the buoyancy of the gasesdthe Earth attracts it less
  4. A body of mass 2\ \text{kg} at rest is acted on by a force of 10\ \text{N} for 3\ \text{s}. The impulse is [1]a6\ \text{N s}b15\ \text{N s}c30\ \text{N s}d60\ \text{N s}
  5. In the free-body diagram above, the block is on the point of sliding. The coefficient of static friction is [1]a\sin\thetab\cos\thetac\tan\thetad1/\tan\theta
  6. Which statement about action and reaction is correct? [1]athey act on the same body and cancelbthey act on different bodies and never cancelcthe action is always largerdthey act at different instants
  7. A man of mass 60\ \text{kg} stands in a lift accelerating upwards at 2\ \text{m s}^{-2} (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). The reading of the weighing machine is [1]a480\ \text{N}b600\ \text{N}c720\ \text{N}d120\ \text{N}
  8. The coefficient of kinetic friction is [1]agreater than the coefficient of static frictionbequal to itcless than itdalways equal to 1
Answers — 2.4

1. (b) — F = ma follows from F = dp/dt only when the mass is constant, which fails for a rocket.

2. (c) — impulse is the change in momentum, so N s = kg m s⁻¹. Option (a) tempts students who read "impulse" as "a big force".

3. (b) — the gas carries momentum backwards, so the rocket carries an equal momentum forwards. Option (a) is the classic error: a rocket works in vacuum, where there is nothing to push against.

4. (c) — J = F\Delta t = 10\times3 = 30\ \text{N s}.

5. (c) — on the point of sliding, f = \mu N, with f = mg\sin\theta and N = mg\cos\theta, so \mu = \tan\theta. This is the angle of repose.

6. (b) — they are equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so they can never be added together to cancel.

7. (c) — N = m(g+a) = 60(12) = 720\ \text{N}. Option (b) is the true weight, chosen by anyone who forgets the lift is accelerating; the machine reads the normal reaction, not the weight.

8. (c) — it always takes a larger force to start sliding than to keep it going.

2.5 Work, energy and power

High-yield fact Value / form
Work W = Fs\cos\theta = \vec F\cdot\vec s; variable force W = \int F\,dx
Power P = W/t = \vec F\cdot\vec v; 1\ \text{hp} = 746\ \text{W}
Work–energy theorem W_{net} = \Delta K
Kinetic energy K = \tfrac12mv^{2} = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}, so p = \sqrt{2mK}
Spring W = \tfrac12kx^{2}
1\ \text{kW h} 3.6\times10^{6}\ \text{J} — a unit of energy
Elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy conserved; equal masses exchange velocities
Perfectly inelastic v = \dfrac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}; KE is lost, momentum is not
  1. The work done by the centripetal force on a body in uniform circular motion is [1]amaximumbzerocnegativedequal to mv^{2}/r
  2. One kilowatt-hour is equal to [1]a1000\ \text{J}b3600\ \text{J}c3.6\times10^{6}\ \text{J}d3.6\times10^{3}\ \text{W}
  3. If the momentum of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes [1]ahalfbdoublecfour timesdunchanged
  4. In a perfectly elastic head-on collision between two bodies of equal mass, one at rest, [1]aboth move togetherbthey exchange velocitiescboth stopdthe moving one rebounds
  5. The work done by a conservative force around any closed path is [1]aalways positivebalways negativeczerodequal to the kinetic energy
  6. A man of mass 60\ \text{kg} climbs a 5\ \text{m} staircase in 10\ \text{s} (g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}). His power output is [1]a30\ \text{W}b300\ \text{W}c3000\ \text{W}d600\ \text{W}
  7. In an inelastic collision, the quantity that is not conserved is [1]alinear momentumbtotal energyckinetic energydmass
  8. A body of mass m and kinetic energy K has linear momentum [1]a\sqrt{2mK}b2mKc\sqrt{mK}dmK^{2}
Answers — 2.5

1. (b) — the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so \cos90^{\circ} = 0. Option (d) is the magnitude of the force, offered to anyone who reads "work" and reaches for the nearest formula.

2. (c) — 1000\ \text{W}\times3600\ \text{s}. Option (d) is the trap: kW h is energy, not power.

3. (c) — K = p^{2}/2m, so K \propto p^{2}. Option (b) comes from assuming K \propto p.

4. (b) — put m_1 = m_2 and u_2 = 0 in the elastic-collision result: v_1 = 0, v_2 = u_1. Option (a) describes a perfectly inelastic collision.

5. (c) — that is the definition of a conservative force.

6. (b) — W = mgh = 60\times10\times5 = 3000\ \text{J}, so P = 3000/10 = 300\ \text{W}. Option (c) is the work, not the power.

7. (c) — momentum and total energy always survive; the missing kinetic energy has become heat, sound and deformation.

8. (a) — invert K = p^2/2m.

2.6 Circular Motion

High-yield fact Value / form
Angular relations v = r\omega, a_t = r\alpha, \omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f
Centripetal acceleration a_c = v^{2}/r = r\omega^{2}
Centripetal force F_c = mv^{2}/r = mr\omega^{2}
Conical pendulum \tan\theta = v^{2}/rg; T_p = 2\pi\sqrt{h/g}
Vertical circle v_{top}^{\min} = \sqrt{gr}, v_{bottom}^{\min} = \sqrt{5gr}, T_2 - T_1 = 6mg
Banking \tan\theta = v^{2}/rg; level road v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu rg}
1\ \text{rpm} 2\pi/60\ \text{rad s}^{-1}
  1. In uniform circular motion, which quantity stays constant? [1]avelocitybspeedcaccelerationdmomentum
  2. The minimum speed at the highest point of a vertical circle of radius r is [1]a\sqrt{gr}b\sqrt{2gr}c\sqrt{5gr}dzero
  3. The difference between the tensions at the lowest and the highest point of a vertical circle is [1]a2mgb3mgc5mgd6mg
  4. A body completes 60 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is [1]a\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}b2\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}c60\ \text{rad s}^{-1}d120\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}
  5. The angle of banking of a road of radius r for a design speed v is given by [1]a\tan\theta = rg/v^{2}b\tan\theta = v^{2}/rgc\sin\theta = v^{2}/rgd\tan\theta = v/rg
  6. The period of a conical pendulum of vertical depth h is [1]a2\pi\sqrt{L/g}b2\pi\sqrt{h/g}c2\pi\sqrt{g/h}d2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/h}
  7. Centrifugal force is [1]athe reaction to the centripetal forceba pseudo-force that appears only in a rotating framecalways greater than the centripetal forceddirected towards the centre
  8. A stone of mass 0.5\ \text{kg} moves in a circle of radius 2\ \text{m} at 4\ \text{m s}^{-1}. The centripetal force is [1]a1\ \text{N}b2\ \text{N}c4\ \text{N}d8\ \text{N}
Answers — 2.6

1. (b) — the direction of velocity changes continuously, so velocity, acceleration and momentum all change; only the magnitude of the velocity is fixed.

2. (a) — at the top, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force when the string goes slack: mg = mv^2/r.

3. (d) — subtracting the two force equations and using v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 4gr gives 6mg, independent of the speed.

4. (b) — 60\ \text{rpm} = 1\ \text{rev s}^{-1} = 2\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}. Option (c) is the trap: rpm read straight off as rad s⁻¹.

5. (b) — from N\sin\theta = mv^2/r and N\cos\theta = mg.

6. (b) — T_p = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}, and L\cos\theta is exactly the depth h below the support.

7. (b) — it is not a real force and has no reaction partner. Option (a) is the commonest wrong answer: the reaction to the centripetal force acts on a different body.

8. (c) — F = mv^2/r = 0.5\times16/2 = 4\ \text{N}.

2.7 Gravitation

High-yield fact Value / form
G 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{kg}^{-2}
Surface value g = GM/R^{2}, so M = gR^{2}/G
Altitude, depth g_h = g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{R}\right) for h\ll R; g_d = g\left(1-\dfrac{d}{R}\right), zero at the centre
Potential, potential energy V = -GM/r (J kg⁻¹), U = -GMm/r
Orbital speed v_o = \sqrt{GM/(R+h)}
Escape velocity v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{2}\,v_o = 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}
Satellite energy K = +\dfrac{GMm}{2r}, U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}, E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}
Geostationary satellite T = 24\ \text{h}, h \approx 36\,000\ \text{km}, equatorial, west to east
  1. The value of g at the centre of the Earth is [1]amaximumbequal to the surface valueczerodinfinite
  2. The escape velocity from the surface of the Earth is approximately [1]a8\ \text{km s}^{-1}b11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}c22.4\ \text{km s}^{-1}d3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}
  3. The escape velocity and the orbital velocity close to the Earth's surface are related by [1]av_e = v_obv_e = 2v_ocv_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_odv_e = v_o/\sqrt{2}
  4. An astronaut inside an orbiting satellite feels weightless because [1]athere is no gravity at that heightbthe astronaut and the satellite are in free fall togethercthe satellite is beyond the atmospheredthe astronaut's mass has become zero
  5. The total energy of a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r is [1]a+GMm/rb-GMm/rc-GMm/2rd+GMm/2r
  6. Escape velocity from a planet does not depend on [1]athe mass of the planetbthe radius of the planetcthe mass of the escaping bodydthe density of the planet
  7. The time period of a geostationary satellite is [1]a1\ \text{h}b12\ \text{h}c24\ \text{h}d365\ \text{days}
  8. Gravitational potential at a point is [1]aalways positivebalways negativeczero everywheredpositive near a mass and negative far from it
Answers — 2.7

1. (c) — g_d = g(1-d/R) gives zero at d = R; only the shell inside your radius pulls you, and at the centre there is none.

2. (b) — v_e = \sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{2\times9.8\times6.4\times10^{6}} \approx 11.2\ \text{km s}^{-1}.

3. (c) — v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} and v_o = \sqrt{GM/R}.

4. (b) — gravity is still about 89\% of its surface value at 400\ \text{km}; what vanishes is the normal reaction. Option (a) is the single commonest misconception in this unit.

5. (c) — E = K+U = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}; it is negative because the satellite is bound.

6. (c) — m cancels out of \tfrac12mv_e^2 = GMm/R.

7. (c) — it must match the Earth's rotation period to stay above the same point.

8. (b) — with V = 0 chosen at infinity and gravity always attractive, V = -GM/r is negative everywhere.

2.8 Elasticity

High-yield fact Value / form
Hooke's law F = kx; k = YA/L, unit N m⁻¹
Young modulus Y = \dfrac{FL}{Ae}, unit Pa = \text{N m}^{-2}
Bulk modulus B = -\dfrac{pV}{\Delta V}; compressibility K = 1/B
Shear modulus \eta = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta}
Poisson's ratio \sigma = \dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}; limits -1 to 0.5; real solids 0.2–0.4
Elastic energy U = \tfrac12Fe; energy density u = \tfrac12\times stress \times strain
Only modulus for fluids bulk modulus
  1. The SI unit of Young modulus is the same as that of [1]aforcebpressurecstraindenergy
  2. Strain has [1]athe unit metrebthe unit newtoncno unit and no dimensionsdthe unit pascal
  3. Which elastic modulus is defined for liquids and gases? [1]aYoung modulusbshear moduluscbulk modulusdall three
  4. The theoretical limits of Poisson's ratio are [1]a0 to 1b-1 to 0.5c-0.5 to 1d0 to \infty
  5. The energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire is [1]astress \times strainb\tfrac12\times stress \times strainc\tfrac12 Y\times stressd\tfrac12\times stress / strain
  6. Breaking stress of a wire depends on [1]aits length onlybits area of cross-section onlycthe material onlydboth its length and its area
  7. Steel is said to be more elastic than rubber because for the same stress steel [1]astretches morebstretches lesscbreaks soonerdis heavier
  8. Hooke's law is obeyed only up to the [1]abreaking pointbyield pointcproportional limitdultimate stress
Answers — 2.8

1. (b) — Y is a stress divided by a dimensionless strain, so it carries the unit of stress, the pascal.

2. (c) — it is a ratio of two lengths (or two volumes). Option (d) is the unit of stress; swapping stress and strain is the classic slip.

3. (c) — fluids have no fixed shape, so they cannot sustain a shear or a tensile stress.

4. (b) — practical materials sit in 0.2–0.4; the negative half of the range belongs to rare auxetic materials.

5. (b) — from U = \tfrac12Fe divided by the volume AL.

6. (c) — breaking stress is a material property; breaking force is what depends on the area.

7. (b) — "more elastic" means a larger Y, i.e. a greater stress is needed per unit strain. Students routinely pick (a) because rubber "stretches more and springs back".

8. (c) — beyond the proportional limit the stress–strain graph is no longer a straight line, even though the wire may still return to its original length up to the elastic limit.

2.9 Heat and Temperature

High-yield fact Value / form
Mean translational KE per molecule \bar E_k = \tfrac32 k_BT — depends on T only

Reading a distractor set before you read the question

Look at question 3 of section 2.22 — three 3\ \mu\text{F} capacitors in series — and notice the shape of the options: 9, 3, 1, 0.33. Those four numbers are not random. 9\ \mu\text{F} is the answer you get with the parallel rule, 3\ \mu\text{F} is what you get if you do nothing at all, 1\ \mu\text{F} is the series answer, and 0.33\ \mu\text{F} is 1/3 of the series answer, i.e. one extra reciprocal step. The examiner has written one option for each of the three commonest errors and one for the truth.

This is worth knowing because it works in reverse. If you can see that the four options are "parallel answer / do-nothing answer / series answer / over-reciprocated answer", you have identified the question as a combination question before you have read a word of the stem, and you know which single fact decides it: for capacitors, series means reciprocals. Spend your twenty seconds confirming that one fact rather than re-deriving the whole thing.

Estimating your way to an optics answer

Question 6 of section 2.17 — a 10\ \text{cm} convex lens with an object at 15\ \text{cm} — has options 6, 30, -30 and 25\ \text{cm}. You can eliminate three of them without touching the lens formula.

The object is between f and 2f, so the standard result applies at once: the image is real, inverted, magnified and lies beyond 2f, that is beyond 20\ \text{cm}. That kills 6\ \text{cm} (too near), kills -30\ \text{cm} (real means positive v for a lens) and leaves 30\ \text{cm} against 25\ \text{cm}. Now one line of arithmetic settles it: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30.

Option 6\ \text{cm} is not an accident either — it is the answer to 1/v = 1/10 + 1/15, i.e. the mirror formula applied to a lens. The examiner put it there for exactly the student who has the two formulas the wrong way round.

Chapter summary

  • Group A of the NEB Physics paper is eleven one-mark objective items drawn from across all twenty-six units, so no unit is safe to skip; the whole of this chapter is built one section per syllabus unit for exactly that reason.
  • Every section opens with a high-yield facts table. Those tables are the smallest thing you can revise that still covers the objective paper: constants, defining formulae, standard values and the one or two named results that MCQs keep returning to.
  • The answer keys give a reason, not a letter. Where an option encodes a standard misconception — mass for weight, the mirror formula for the lens formula, the resistor rule for the capacitor rule, zero field for zero potential, mass defect for binding energy — the key names it, because recognising your own error is worth more than recognising the right answer.
  • Recurring traps to carry into the hall: unit prefixes (μ, m, k) left unconverted; \text{kW h} treated as a power; c_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T} read as linear; the \tfrac12 in capacitor energy; the sign convention in mirror and lens problems; \tfrac32kT per molecule versus \tfrac32RT per mole; weightlessness explained as "no gravity".
  • Objective marks are the cheapest marks in the paper and the easiest to throw away. One minute per item is the budget; if an item resists for longer, mark it, move on, and come back after Group C.
